paragraphs.text: Pedestrian crossings with traffic lights were first introduced to reduce accidents, but their design has changed a great deal since then. Early crossings gave walkers a fixed amount of time, which many older people found too short.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Modern crossings in several cities use sensors that detect when someone is still in the road and keep the traffic lights red until they reach the pavement. In trials, this reduced the number of people still crossing when cars began to move by more than half.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Countdown timers, which show how many seconds are left, have had mixed results. They helped pedestrians decide whether to start crossing, but some drivers used them to judge when to speed up, which increased the risk to people who crossed late.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Sound signals were added to help people with poor sight. Some cities now use a different sound for each direction of the crossing, so that users know which way it is safe to walk.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Researchers stress that crossings work best when they are placed where people actually want to cross. If a crossing is too far from shops or bus stops, many pedestrians simply cross elsewhere.
paragraphs.label: E
